source_text: Sed et Timotheo scribens, vult juvenculas nubere, filios suscipere, matres familiae agere. Ad eas dirigit, quales supra denotat, juvenculas viduas, quae in viduitate deprehensae, et aliquandiu adsectatae, postquam in deliciis habuerunt Christum, nubere volunt, habentes judicium quod primam fidem resciderunt: illam videlicet, a qua in viduitate inventae, et professae eam, non perseverant. Propter quod vult eas nubere, ne primam fidem susceptae viduitatis postea rescindant, non ut totiens nubant, quotieas in viduitate tentata, imo et in deliciis habita noluerint perseverare. Legimus eum et ad Romanos scribentem: Quae autem sub viro est mulier, viventi viro vincta est; si autem obierit, evacuata est a lege viri. Nempe ergo vivente viro adulterare putabitur, si juncta fuerit alteri viro. Si vero obierit vir, liberata est a lege, quod non sit adultera facta alii viro. Sed et sequentia recognosce, quo sensus iste, qui tibi blanditur, evadat: Itaque, inquit, fratres mei, mortificamini et vos legi per corpus Christi, ut efficiamini alteri, ei scilicet qui a mortuis resurrexit, uti fructum feramus Deo. Cum enim eramus in carne, passiones delictorum, quae per legem efficiebantur in membris nostris ad fructum ferendum morti: nunc autem evacuati sumus a lege, mortui in quo tenebamur, ad serviendum Deo in novitate spiritus, et non in vetustate literae. Igitur, si mortificari nos jubet legi per corpus Christi, quod est Ecclesia, quae spiritu novitatis constat, non per literam vetustatis, id est legis; auferens te a lege, quae non tenet uxorem, marito defuncto, quominus alii viro fiat, ad contrariam te redigit conditionem, ne, amisso viro, nubas; quantumque non deputareris adultera facta alteri viro post mortem mariti, si adhuc in lege agere deberes, tanto ex diversitate conditionis adulterii te praejudicat post mortem mariti alii nubentem: quia jam mortificata es legi, non potest tibi licere, cum recessisti ab ea apud quam tibi licebat.
pass_a_gloss: But also writing to Timothy, he wants young women to marry, to have children, to manage a household. He directs this to those kinds of young women, widows, whom he described above, who were caught in widowhood and for some time followed it, but after they had Christ as their delight, they want to marry, having a judgment that they had rescinded their first faith, that is, the one from which they were found in widowhood and had professed, but do not persevere in it. On account of this, he wants them to marry, lest they later rescind the first faith of the widowhood they had undertaken, not so that they may marry as many times as they were tempted in widowhood and even in delight did not want to persevere. We read him also writing to the Romans: A woman who is under a husband is bound to the living husband; if indeed the husband dies, she is freed from the law of the husband. Therefore, she will be considered an adulteress if she is joined to another husband while the husband is living. But if the husband dies, she is freed from the law, so that she is not made an adulteress by another husband. But also recognize the following, by which this sense, which flatters you, escapes: Therefore, he says, my brothers, let us also mortify the law through the body of Christ, so that we may be made suitable for another, that is, the one who rose from the dead, so that we may bear fruit for God. For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were effective in our members through the law for bearing fruit for death, now however we are freed from the law, having died to that in which we were held, to serve God in newness of spirit and not in oldness of letter. Therefore, if he commands us to mortify the law through the body of Christ, which is the Church, which consists in the spirit of newness and not in the letter of oldness, that is, the law, taking you away from the law, which does not hold a wife, with the husband deceased, from becoming another's wife, he leads you to a contrary condition, so that, having lost a husband, you do not marry; and as much as you would not be considered an adulteress, made to another husband after the death of the husband, if you still had to act according to the law, so much does he prejudge you, marrying another after the death of the husband, due to the diversity of the condition of adultery, because now you have been mortified to the law, it cannot be permitted to you, since you have departed from that according to which it was permitted to you.
pass_b_english: When Paul writes to Timothy, he tells younger widows to marry, have children, and run a household (1 Tim 5:14). He addresses the very women he described earlier: widows who once committed to celibacy, stuck with it for a while, but then — after tasting Christ as their delight — decide they want to marry again. By doing so they pass sentence on themselves: they have broken their first pledge, the very faith that led them into widowhood and that they publicly professed, yet they do not persevere in it. That is precisely why Paul urges them to marry — not so they can rack up husbands every time widowhood tests them and they refuse to hold fast even in delight, but to keep them from later renouncing the original vow they took when they embraced widowhood.

We also find Paul writing to the Romans: "A married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of marriage" (Rom 7:2–3). So if she joins another man while her husband is alive, she will be called an adulteress; but if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and marrying another man does not make her an adulteress (Rom 7:3). Now follow the next lines closely, so the interpretation that flatters you can be exposed. Paul says, "Therefore, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who was raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God" (Rom 7:4). He explains: "For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death. But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code" (Rom 7:5–6).

If Paul commands us to die to the law through the body of Christ — and that body is the Church, which lives by the Spirit of newness, not by the letter of the old law — then he is pulling you out of the very law that releases a widow to remarry after her husband's death. He drives you into the opposite condition: having lost your husband, you must not marry. Under the old law you would not be counted an adulteress for marrying again after your husband's death; but precisely because you have now died to that law, the new condition brands you an adulteress if you remarry. You have departed from the law that once gave you permission, so that permission no longer applies.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological argument regarding the transition from the law to the spirit. Pass A provides a literal rendering of the Latin, while Pass B provides a fluent English version that correctly identifies and expands the scripture citations (1 Tim 5:14, Rom 7:2-6) which were present in the Latin text as allusions/quotes. All clauses, including the conditional argument at the end, are preserved.
source: 'in deliciis habuerunt Christum'; English: 'had Christ as their delight'
